column1: Define date boundaries with {{c1::CREATE PARTITION FUNCTION}} PF_OrderDate(DATETIME2) AS RANGE RIGHT FOR VALUES ('20240101', '20240401');
column2:
The function defines how values map to partitions, not their filegroups.
Review source

column1: Map PF_OrderDate to storage with {{c1::CREATE PARTITION SCHEME}} PS_OrderDate AS PARTITION PF_OrderDate ALL TO ([PRIMARY]);
column2:
The partition function must already exist.
Review source

column1: In a partition scheme, {{c1::ALL TO ([PRIMARY])}} maps every partition to the PRIMARY filegroup.
column2:
Several partitions can share one filegroup. Azure SQL Database and Fabric SQL database require all partitions on PRIMARY.
Review source

column1: Place a table on PS_OrderDate using OrderDate as its partitioning column with the final clause {{c1::ON PS_OrderDate(OrderDate)}}.
column2:
This clause supplies the scheme and its input column in CREATE TABLE.
Review source

column1: A partition function with four distinct boundary values creates {{c1::five partitions}}.
column2:
The number of partitions is the number of boundaries plus one.
Review source

column1: For RANGE RIGHT FOR VALUES (100, 200), the value 100 maps to partition {{c1::2}}.
column2:
The first partition contains values below 100.
Review source

column1: For RANGE LEFT FOR VALUES (100, 200), the value 100 maps to partition {{c1::1}}.
column2:
The first partition includes its upper boundary of 100.
Review source

column1: If neither LEFT nor RIGHT is specified in a partition function, SQL Server uses {{c1::RANGE LEFT}}.
column2:
Explicitly state the range direction to make boundary ownership clear.
Review source

column1: For a DATETIME2 function using RANGE RIGHT with final boundary '20241001', the last partition has {{c1::no later explicit boundary}}.
column2:
It includes valid DATETIME2 dates from October 1, 2024 onward, not just that year's fourth quarter.
Review source

column1: For a clustered primary key partitioned on PS_OrderDate(OrderDate), use PRIMARY KEY (OrderID, {{c1::OrderDate}}).
column2:
A partitioned unique index must include its partitioning column in the index key.
Review source

column1: PRIMARY KEY (OrderID, OrderDate) enforces uniqueness of {{c1::the column pair}}, not OrderID alone.
column2:
Adding a partitioning column changes the key's uniqueness rule.
Review source

column1: Given dbo.Orders uses PS_OrderDate(OrderDate), align its index with CREATE INDEX IX_Customer ON dbo.Orders(CustomerID) {{c1::ON PS_OrderDate(OrderDate)}};
column2:
For a nonunique nonclustered index, SQL Server can add the partitioning column as an included column.
Review source

column1: Given partition function PF_OrderDate, locate a date with SELECT {{c1::$PARTITION}}.PF_OrderDate('20240515');
column2:
The result depends on the boundaries and range direction of the existing PF_OrderDate function.
Review source

column1: Count rows per nonempty partition with SELECT $PARTITION.PF_OrderDate(OrderDate), COUNT(*) FROM dbo.Orders {{c1::GROUP BY $PARTITION.PF_OrderDate(OrderDate)}};
column2:
Empty partitions do not appear in a grouping query over stored rows.
Review source

column1: Given a new boundary and schemes ready for a split, use ALTER PARTITION FUNCTION PF_OrderDate() {{c1::SPLIT RANGE}} ('20250101');
column2:
This adds one boundary and one partition.
Review source

column1: For PF_OrderDate with existing boundary '20240401', remove it with ALTER PARTITION FUNCTION PF_OrderDate() {{c1::MERGE RANGE}} ('20240401');
column2:
The removed boundary must exist, and the rows remain in the merged partition.
Review source

column1: Prepare PS_OrderDate to receive another partition on PRIMARY with ALTER PARTITION SCHEME PS_OrderDate {{c1::NEXT USED [PRIMARY]}};
column2:
This designates storage for the new partition created by SPLIT RANGE.
Review source

column1: Before SPLIT RANGE, every partition scheme using the function must have a {{c1::NEXT USED filegroup}}.
column2:
A scheme without this designation causes the split to fail.
Review source

column1: Assuming SWITCH requirements are met, archive partition 2 with ALTER TABLE dbo.Orders {{c1::SWITCH}} PARTITION 2 TO dbo.OrdersArchive;
column2:
The archive table must already exist, be empty, and satisfy the structural and storage requirements.
Review source

column1: Rebuild only partition 3 of a partitioned IX_Customer index with ALTER INDEX IX_Customer ON dbo.Orders REBUILD {{c1::PARTITION = 3}};
column2:
This does not rebuild every partition of the index.
Review source

column1: Create per-partition statistics on an eligible partitioned table with CREATE STATISTICS ST_OrderDate ON dbo.Orders(OrderDate) WITH {{c1::INCREMENTAL = ON}};
column2:
Partitioning alone does not automatically enable incremental statistics.
Review source

column1: Choose daily, monthly, or yearly partition intervals according to {{c1::data volume and retention needs}}.
column2:
There is no universally best interval for every table.
Review source

column1: With an enabled columnstore index on a table, SPLIT RANGE requires the partition being split to be {{c1::empty}}.
column2:
Prepare future boundaries before data fills the partition.
Review source

column1: Different partition-function names can still allow index alignment when their definitions are {{c1::equivalent}}.
column2:
Match input types, partition counts, boundary values, and RANGE LEFT or RANGE RIGHT behavior.
Review source
